tagline.text: Manila's biggest wholesale market, where every day starts with haggling

children.text: The Philippines' largest wholesale market district, spread between Tondo and Binondo in Manila. At 168 Shopping Mall, 999 Shopping Mall, Tutuban Center and the street stalls, the fun lies in haggling for clothes, toys, household goods and Christmas decorations at close to wholesale prices.

Divisoria is a commercial district of about 0.5㎢ spanning three Manila districts, Tondo, Binondo and San Nicolas, and Filipinos fondly call this mecca of budget shopping "Divi." True to its Spanish name, meaning "dividing place," it was the boundary in the Spanish era between the walled city of Intramuros and the Parián, where Chinese traders lived, and Chinese merchants' businesses grew along this line. Many shop owners are still Chinese Filipinos, and Binondo Chinatown is a
10–15-minute
walk to the south.

The main road cutting east to west through the middle of the district is Recto Avenue (C.M. Recto Avenue), and alleys such as Juan Luna, Ylaya, Tabora, Santo Cristo and Santa Elena streets branch off it like a spider's web to the north and south. Tutuban station, the starting point of the Manila–Dagupan railway that opened in
, drew in trade and goods; the area declined after World War II but came back to life in the
, starting with Tutuban Center and followed by large shopping arcades such as 168 Shopping Mall, 999 Shopping Mall and Divisoria Mall.

You can find almost anything imaginable here. Clothes and shoes, bags, toys, school supplies, party goods, fabric and sewing materials, kitchenware, phone accessories, packaging and baking supplies, fruit, vegetables and dried fish are all sold, with each street specializing in its own goods. Because it is a wholesale market where small shop owners and provincial store keepers stock up, prices drop further when you buy several pieces, and regular customers (suki) get better deals. In peak season hundreds of thousands of people come in a day, so you need to be prepared for crowds, heat and pickpockets.

It is recommended for travelers who want to see the unvarnished face of Manila's working-class economy, a world away from luxury malls. Korean residents of the Philippines have long loved it as the place to stock up cheaply on school event supplies, shop equipment, and Christmas gifts and decorations all at once. With Binondo Chinatown and Quiapo Church nearby, it combines well into a half-day or full-day route: shopping in Divisoria in the morning and a food crawl in Binondo in the afternoon.

blocks.title: Exploring the maze of 168 Shopping Mall

children.text: Opened in

on Soler Street, 168 Shopping Mall is Divisoria's flagship arcade, with hundreds of small stalls packed into several wings. The ground floor has household items and gift knickknacks such as tumblers and fans, while the upper floors gather toys, party goods, clothes and shoes; it is easy to get lost, so remember the name of the entrance you came in through.

blocks.title: Picking bags and travel gear at 999 Shopping Mall

children.text: 999 Shopping Mall, with its yellow and green facade right behind 168 Shopping Mall, labels each aisle with a letter (Pasilyo A, B …), making it easier to navigate than 168. It has lots of bags, luggage, slippers and stuffed toys; faux-leather bags start at about
and waterproof backpacks cost about

blocks.title: Tutuban Center and the old railway station

children.text: This shopping center preserves the old Tutuban station building, whose cornerstone was laid in

; its aisles are wider than other arcades and its food courts and restrooms are clean, making it a good starting point for shopping in Divisoria. It is full of home goods such as curtains, cushions and fabric, plus casual clothing, and in front of the main entrance stands a monument to the revolutionary Andrés Bonifacio, who was born near here.

blocks.title: Gift and fabric alleys of Ylaya Street

children.text: Ylaya Street is an alley lined with shops selling gift items, party materials, fabric, handicrafts and kitchenware. Slippers cost around
and shoes go up to about
, so many people come here for group souvenirs and event giveaways.

blocks.title: Specialist wholesalers on Tabora and Santo Cristo streets

children.text: Tabora Street gathers costumes, party goods, sewing materials and home decor, while Santo Cristo Street is home to wholesalers of packaging, disposable tableware, baking supplies and kitchenware. Mingling with locals buying ingredients by the box for small eateries and home baking, you can feel the wholesale market atmosphere at its most intense.

blocks.title: Getting a dress fitted at Dragon 8

children.text: Dragon 8 Shopping Center (D8) on Recto Avenue is an arcade specializing in party dresses and formal wear, where in-house seamstresses take in garments on the spot. Cocktail dresses are said to start at about
and wedding gowns at about
, but prices vary greatly from shop to shop.

blocks.title: Fruit and vegetable wholesalers and the night market on Recto Avenue

children.text: Fruit and vegetable wholesalers line Recto Avenue and the surrounding alleys, and from dusk a night market selling clothes, sundries and fruit sets up. The night market's area and hours change often under the city of Manila's street-vendor rules, so check on site.
In
November–December

the whole district is covered with Christmas decorations, parol star lanterns, toys, gift tumblers and mugs, and groceries for the Christmas Eve feast (Noche Buena). At year's end it fills up again with people buying 12 kinds of round fruit and charms for luck in the new year.

items.title: From the airport and other cities

children.text: From other islands such as Cebu or Davao, the simplest way is to fly to Manila on a domestic flight and take a Grab straight here. If you come up by bus from the south, such as Batangas or Cavite, you can ride LRT Line 1 from PITX Station next to the PITX terminal to Doroteo Jose Station without changing trains. The Philippine National Railways (PNR) Metro Manila service that ran to Tutuban station has been suspended since
March 28, 2024
for construction of the North–South Commuter Railway, with resumption planned for around
late 2028 to early 2029
From Binondo Church, walk north about
along Juan Luna Street or Santo Cristo Street,
10–15 minutes
, to reach 168 Shopping Mall. From Quiapo Church it takes about
20–25 minutes
via Carriedo Street and Recto Avenue. The streets are narrow and busy with crowds and carts, so it is safer to learn the route beforehand rather than walk while staring at a map app.
Divisoria is open year-round, but since you will walk for a long time along shadeless stall-lined streets, the
November–February
dry season is the most comfortable time. In
March–May
midday temperatures reach
and the alleys turn into a steam bath, so move around between
8 and 10 AM
, when the shops open. In the
June–October
rainy season, afternoon showers and typhoons are frequent, and low-lying alleys flood quickly in heavy rain.
The busiest time of the year is the Christmas rush. From
mid-December
until Christmas Eve, office workers and families flock here after their last payday, so it is hard even to walk, and some arcades extend their hours to stay open late into the night. Then in
late December
, before the new year, it fills up again with people buying round fruit, lucky charms and firecrackers. In
May–June
, before school starts, it is packed with parents buying school supplies. If you want to browse in peace, avoid these periods and go on a weekday morning.

There is almost nowhere for travelers to stay inside Divisoria, and the streets go dark after the arcades close in the evening. The nearest options are Hotel Lucky Chinatown and Ramada by Wyndham Manila Central in Binondo, a
10–15-minute
walk away (about
a night), but most travelers stay in Ermita, Malate or Makati and visit as a day trip. If you expect to buy a lot, choose a place you can drive straight up to.

Many people eat simply at the food courts of arcades such as Tutuban Center and 168 Shopping Mall. Along the streets, stalls selling skewered fried snacks such as fish balls and kikiam, turon (banana wrapped in spring roll wrapper and fried), coconut juice (buko) and sugarcane juice keep hunger at bay while you shop. For a proper meal, head south to Binondo for the Chinese-style fried chicken at Sincerity, open since
, or a dumpling shop on Ongpin Street, and pick up hopia from Eng Bee Tin, founded in
, as a dessert gift. If you need an air-conditioned break, Lucky Chinatown Mall on Reina Regente Street in Binondo is also close by.
Most arcades open around
8 AM
and close around
7 PM
. Many small shops close on Sundays, so a weekday morning is best.

Haggling is expected. Don't buy right after asking the price; check two or three shops selling the same item, then offer a little less than the first price with a smile. Many shops will drop close to wholesale prices if you buy several of the same item.
That said, if you see something you like, it is better to buy it on the spot. Similar shops go on endlessly, and it is very hard to find a shop again once you have passed it.
Most places accept cash only.
bills are often refused for lack of change, so bring plenty of small bills of
and split your money among several places.

Bring a close-fitting crossbody or belt bag and a reusable shopping bag, and wear comfortable sneakers and quick-drying clothes. Many locals wear a thin, close-fitting top so they can try clothes on over it.

Stalls and small shops rarely have fitting rooms, and exchanges or refunds are difficult. Bring a tape measure for clothing sizes, check zippers and stitching on bags, and test electronics on the spot.

When asking prices, add the polite "po," as in "How much po?", and at the end ask politely, "Last price po?" Haggling too hard, or walking away without buying after agreeing on a price, is considered rude.
Bring water, a hat and a portable fan, and use the restroom beforehand in Tutuban Center or a large arcade. There are almost no restrooms on the stall-lined streets.

Divisoria is one of the worst places in Manila for pickpockets, so much so that police deploy extra officers every Christmas season. Carry your bag in front of you, never put your phone in a back pocket, and do not wear valuable accessories such as necklaces or watches.

A common trick is to drop coins, say something has stained your clothes, or deliberately bump into you, then rob your bag while you are distracted. If a stranger suddenly approaches, check your bag first.
At year's end, some stalls secretly sell banned firecrackers (piccolo, pla-pla and others), and police have arrested sellers in crackdowns. They are both dangerous and illegal, so do not buy them.

Most clothes, bags and shoes bearing famous brand names are not genuine. Counterfeits may be confiscated under the customs rules of the country you return to, so choose by usefulness rather than label.
Motorcycles, tricycles and handcarts squeeze through the crowds in the alleys. Do not look at your phone while walking, and hold children's hands firmly.
Avoid dark alleys after the arcades close; if you go to the night market, stay on the main road and take a Grab home. If you have a sensitive stomach, avoid ice in street drinks.
